tagline: A one-page letter from the elder to a chosen lady and her children, urging love that walks in God's commands and a door closed to teachers who deny Christ came in the flesh.
overview:
Second John is, by word count, the second shortest book in the Bible after Third John, thirteen verses that would fit on a single sheet of papyrus. It comes from a writer who calls himself simply “The elder” and is addressed to “the chosen lady and her children”. The elder is glad to hear that some of her children are walking in the truth. He reminds her of the commandment they have had from the beginning, that we love one another, and he defines that love as walking according to God's commands.

Then comes the warning that gives the letter its urgency. Many deceivers have gone out into the world who refuse to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. The lady and her household must not lose what has been worked for, and they must not give such teachers a welcome or a platform. The letter closes with the hope of a visit face to face.

Small as it is, Second John shows how the concerns of First John played out in the ordinary life of a house church: who gets welcomed, who gets hosted, and how love and truth are held together when a community's doors are open to travelers.
author: The writer identifies himself only as the elder (Greek presbyteros, which can mean an older man or a church leader). Early Christian tradition identified him with John the apostle, author of the Gospel and of First John, and the vocabulary and themes of this letter (truth, love, abiding, the commandment from the beginning, the antichrist, Christ come in the flesh) match First John so closely that almost all scholars assign the three letters to the same author or circle. Whether the elder is the apostle himself or another leader named John, sometimes identified with the John the elder mentioned by Papias in the early second century, is debated. The title suggests a senior figure whose authority was recognized across several congregations without needing further explanation.
date: Like First John, the letter is usually dated late in the first century, around AD 85 to 100. Its concerns, especially the deceivers who deny Christ's coming in the flesh, match those of First John, and the two letters were probably written close in time. Some scholars think Second John came first, as a brief warning later expanded; most think First John was written first or at about the same time.
setting:
The church met in a household, and the letter concerns the running of that household. Early Christian mission depended on hospitality: traveling teachers, prophets, and missionaries moved between towns and relied on believers to house and feed them. That system spread the gospel quickly, but it also spread false teaching, because anyone could arrive claiming to speak for Christ. The deceivers of verse 7 belong to the same movement as the secessionists of 1 John 2:19, people who had left the fellowship and were now traveling with a teaching that denied the full humanity of Jesus, very likely an early form of docetism, the belief that the divine Christ only seemed to have a body.

Who the chosen lady is remains open. Many interpreters take her as a figure for a local church, with her children as its members and her elect sister (verse 13) as the church where the elder is. Others think she was a real Christian woman, perhaps a patron who hosted a church in her home. The Greek word kyria, lady, was also used as a personal name, and a few have suggested reading it that way.
purpose: The elder writes to encourage a congregation that is walking in the truth, to remind it of the command to love, and above all to warn it against giving hospitality and support to the traveling teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. He wants the church to keep what it has received rather than running ahead into a new teaching that leaves Christ behind (verse 9).
story: Second John belongs to the last decades of the first century, when the church had spread across the Roman world and the generation of eyewitnesses was passing. It stands with First and Third John as a window into the churches connected with the apostle John in the province of Asia. The same Christ who, in John's Gospel, became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14) is here the dividing line in the church's life: to remain in his teaching is to have both the Father and the Son. Third John, which follows, shows the other side of the hospitality question, a church leader refusing to welcome faithful missionaries.
christ: The letter's center is the confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. For the elder, the incarnation is not a detail to be adjusted but the heart of the faith: God's Son truly became human. Denying it is the mark of the deceiver and the antichrist (verse 7). Whoever remains in the teaching about Christ has both the Father and the Son (verse 9). The letter also links truth and love in Christ: grace, mercy, and peace come from the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love (verse 3).
reading: Read Second John with First John open beside it, since the short letter assumes the argument of the longer one. Notice how often the word truth appears; it is not a set of propositions only but a reality that abides in believers and in which they walk. The instruction not to receive or greet a false teacher (verses 10-11) is often misread as permission for general rudeness or for shunning anyone who disagrees. In context it concerns traveling teachers who deny the incarnation and who would use a church's hospitality as a base for their teaching. The elder's concern is not private disagreement but public sponsorship of a message that empties the gospel.

structure.title: Greeting in truth and love
structure.summary: The elder greets the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in the truth, with grace, mercy, and peace from the Father and the Son.

structure.title: Walking in truth and love
structure.summary: He rejoices that some of her children walk in the truth and reminds her of the old commandment that we love one another, which means walking in God's commands.

structure.title: Deceivers and the doctrine of Christ
structure.summary: Many deceivers deny Jesus Christ come in the flesh. The church must hold to the teaching of Christ and not welcome or support those who bring another teaching.

structure.title: Closing: hope of a visit
structure.summary: The elder has more to say but hopes to speak face to face, and he sends greetings from the children of the elect sister.

themes.title: Truth
themes.body: The word appears five times in the first four verses. Truth is something believers know, something that abides in them and will be with them forever, and something they walk in. It is finally bound to the person of Christ, and so it cannot be separated from what one believes about him.

themes.title: Love as obedience
themes.body: The elder defines love by action: this is love, that we walk according to his commandments (verse 6). Love is not a feeling set against God's commands but the life those commands describe. It is also the old command, heard from the beginning, not a new discovery.

themes.title: Christ come in the flesh
themes.body: The test of true teaching is the incarnation. Those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh have gone beyond the teaching of Christ and do not have God. The letter shows how central the full humanity of Jesus was to the earliest church.

themes.title: Hospitality and discernment
themes.body: The church's open door was one of its great strengths. The elder does not close it; he asks the church to discern whom it sends out with its blessing. Welcome is a form of partnership, and the church must not partner with a message that denies Christ.

keyChapters.why: The whole letter: truth and love held together, and the warning against teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
